It appears to have gone now, but I notice there is still an old sign on the wall in Mattock Lane pointing to a library. I have two memories about a park which may or may not have been Walpole Park; if not I can't think which. I remember time and again running through waist-high autumn leaves. name: Keats House
reviews: [{'language': 'en', 'polarity': 5, 'rating': 0, 'source': 'Foursquare', 'text': 'See the rooms where Keats lived when he wrote "Ode to a Nightingale," then go for a walk on Hampstead Heath. Who knows what inspiration you\'ll find?', 'time': '2012-05-27', 'wordsCount': 27}, {'language': 'en', 'polarity': 10, 'rating': 0, 'source': 'Foursquare', 'text': 'Great people', 'time': '2013-03-02', 'wordsCount': 2}, {'language': 'en', 'polarity': 9, 'rating': 5, 'source': 'GooglePlaces', 'text': 'With so many Ã¼ber bars, venues and pop-up restaurants around it's easy to forget what (I think) really makes London so unique: the fascinating history lurking around every corner. So it's a good job that people like 'London Shh' (Secret Historic Houses) exist to take care of these significant places while we're off enjoying another prohibition-style cocktail in Shoreditch, or signing up to the waiting list for the 68th floor of The Shard. Hiding down seemingly regular streets all over town are the former residences of some of history's more notable personalities, including Benjamin Franklin, Lucien Freud and John Keats, all carefully maintained and kept open to the public by London Shh. The latter (Keats) once resided in a fairly modest house in Hampstead, 'Wentworth Place', where he wrote some of his most famous poems and met the love of his life Fanny Brawne, and it's among the nine houses open to the public (pick up a 'Shh' loyalty card if this sort of thing is your bag!) Keats House is a place which you might otherwise walk by, especially in well-to-do Hampstead, where many of the buildings have something of the impressive about them, but in this pretty white building, next to the local library, you can see Keats' parlour, where wrote 'Ode to a Nightingale', his bedroom and even his wine cellar. The house hosts alternating exhibitions, which have included love letters to Fanny Brawne and, currently, his annotated copy of Shakespeare's works and Fanny's rather bling engagement ring. What's more, if you are so inclined, they also run sewing workshops, where you can find a cosy spot anywhere in the house and make yourself an empire line dress / Regency jacket / bonnet. Something to sport for your next trip to the aforementioned Shoreditch cocktail bar perhapsâ€¦ The spirit of Keats House's former inhabitants is very much alive, and visiting is an eye-opening experience, as well as the perfect way to legitimately indulge in some good old-fashioned nosiness. The poor man died at the age of 25, having never married Fanny, and wandering around his old quarters makes you appreciate how much he accomplished in his very short life. Hampstead might be a bit far for some Londoners to travel, but there are open houses all over town. I spoke to their team to find out if there is any chance to terminate my membership any sooner if I pay some cancellation fee which I was hopping to be less then paying for all remaining months. I explained I never used any of my membership benefits (free tennis or sqoash lesssons) and was hoping for some understanding and good business manner. I have been promised that manager will call me to solve this problem, what never happened, so I kept paying them for 8 months not using the club at all. Then, I went there to give - as I have been informed - 1 month notice and find out that I didn't make it on time for their billing period so now I'll have to pay them for next 3 months! I find it very unfair, but reception is unable to deal with this issue, a manager never calls back (I requested it 3 times till now) and there's no e-mail address or any other instance to make a formal complaint. Now, I do understand that fixed term contracts are widely used by gyms and sport clubs, I know what I signed for but there are some circumstances that should be taken into consideration and some exemptions to be made. Long story short, I am paying over Â£100 per month for a service I have no way of using. Great Food, Lounge with Sky...', 'time': '2012-07-05', 'wordsCount': 14}, {'language': 'en', 'polarity': 8, 'rating': 4, 'source': 'GooglePlaces', 'text': 'Reports of New Docklands Steam Club are very polarised - from uncomplimentary to flattering so I decided I needed to pay a visit and find out for myself. True, its location is not the most pretty - on an industrial estate, bounded by rail tracks and flyovers ... that can't be helped - it's an accident of history. The building and its interior are definitely "no frills" but the staff made us welcome and were courteous. The reputation that regular users are unfriendly to newbies was proven untrue - there were friendly guys to chat to. This is a real baths - not high end 5 star health spa. The steam rooms and sauna provide some serious heat with ample scope for scrubbing and massage. I was glad I was able to buy a proper felt sauna hat - it was a godsend in the sauna! I have wanted one for ages instead of wearing a wooly bobble hat. Finally the food - had a lovely meal at reasonable cost. In conclusion, it was worth the time and cost of going ..... it was a good experience ..... I would go back and also recommend others go ...... if you open your mind and realise you are entering a different world. It's an old building so can't be easy or cheap to maintain while holding costs at something sensible. Finally .... don't wait to be spoken to .... extending a friendly "hello" broke down barriers. Admittedly there will be groups of cliquey regulars who meet up there .... the schmeissing brigade! But you'll get that in any pub or other social insitution. All in all, a pleasant surprise (given some of what I had heard!) and I shall be back. This establishment is certainly unique in the UK and needs to be supported. Incidentally the location on Google maps isn't quite right - it is actually opposite Wickes depot, not at the end of the street as marked.', 'time': '2011-08-19', 'wordsCount': 331}]

name: Jewish Military Museum
address: Shield House, Harmony Way, London, United Kingdom
reviews: [{'language': 'en', 'polarity': 5, 'rating': 4, 'source': 'GooglePlaces', 'text': 'A tiny museum packing a big punch. The Jewish Military Museum is a real hidden gem. Tucked away off the high street 10 minutes walk from Hendon Central, this museum can be tricky to find, but don't let that put you off. If you are at all interested in military history or Jewish culture this is a fantastic museum to visit. It's charm lies in it's uniqueness. All the donations to the museum tell stories about the lives of those who donated them. And there is a wide range of stories being told here, from WWI through to present day military conflicts, the people represented range from soldiers, to firemen, to the home front, to womens' service and more. The museum holds some lovely donations including uniforms, letters to loved ones at home from the front lines, photographs, medals, trinkets and more. Well worth a visit. Make sure you phone or email to let the museum know you are coming, so they can put your name on the door.', 'time': '2013-05-15', 'wordsCount': 171}]

name: Ragged School Museum
reviews: [{'language': 'en', 'polarity': 8, 'rating': 5, 'source': 'GooglePlaces', 'text': 'I visited during the free summer holiday activity weeks and fell in love with this place. There are only a few members of staff and a lot of volunteers keeping this unique venue open. Some of the volunteers have been there for many years but they still love the place and still enjoy showing someone new the delights. There are four floors to explore with a local history museum on the ground floor, a Victorian classroom plus the Art Room on the first floor and the top floor has a kitchen where children can try and beat a rug, peg washing on a line, etc. The basement has a cafe that opens onto the Regent's Canal and a large soft play room for younger visitors. I visit a lot of museums that profess to be child-friendly but this place wins hands-down and I can't wait to go back. reviews: [{'language': 'en', 'polarity': 2, 'rating': 1, 'source': 'GooglePlaces', 'text': 'I liked the Heart & Soul Fitness space. After that she seems to forget that you may not want to renew your membership thereafter. (possibly due to the low fee nature of the gym, she is reliant on having new clientele through the doors each month and not as bothered with the returning custom.) reviews: [{'language': 'en', 'polarity': 8, 'rating': 5, 'source': 'GooglePlaces', 'text': 'I've been a member of the Gym Clinic for around a year and a half and in that time the gym has gone from strength to strength. It is a professionally operated, private gym that caters for both novices and advance trainees. The gym itself has a number of cardio machines including treadmills, spinning bikes, cross trainers, rowing machine and step machine - along with this it has a full range of resistance machines to work every major muscle group. The machines themselves are placed in an organised location and are very accessible to new trainees who may find some free weight exercises quite daunting. The gym also has a boxing ring where classes/ 1-2-1 sessions are held for a variety of trainee levels and ages - a great edition to any gym and gives the members something you won't find in most privately run places. The free weights area boast 3 benches, an adjustable bench press going from 180 to 90 degrees, dual cable machines with a variety of attachments, a squat rack with optional safety mechanisms and a 3D 'Jones Machine' which offers the safety of a 'Smith Machine' but with lateral movement as well as vertical. Along with these machines there are free weights ranging from 1kg up to 50kg, weight plates from 1.25kg to 25kg and assorted barbells. Lastly there is a small area outside that has a number of punching bags as well as some tyres and sledge hammers so that trainees can try some more unique approaches to cardio/strength training. The kit itself is in fantastic condition, with the cardio and resistance machines being brand new and top of the range - while also being divided into approachable locations so that new members and trainees should not feel any intimidation with using any of the equipment; especially since they all have instructions on how best to use the machines. The members are incredibly friendly, and the gym has a family vibe to it - where people of all levels mix and help create an atmosphere that is both welcoming and pleasant to exercise in. This aspect is certainly something that gives the gym clinic an edge to commercial gyms where most members are anonymous to each other; never really exchanging pleasantries or training experiences - certainly not the case here. Though despite the professional kit the gym carries, it is certainly not a 'male' gym - the membership is split quite evenly between men and women which again helps create an inviting atmosphere. The gym comes with locker facilities as well as 3 small showers that are cleaned regularly. My only criticism would be some of the lockers are faulty and so it can be difficult to find a spare locker from time to time; but this is hardly much of an issue. name: Hoopers Gallery
reviews: [{'language': 'en', 'polarity': 8, 'rating': 5, 'source': 'GooglePlaces', 'text': 'The British Wildlife Photography Awards 2010. On Tuesday 26th October, my family and I went to the Hoopers Gallery in Clerkenwell Close, London. I went to visit an exhibition of photographs submitted in for the British Wildlife Photography Award 2010. The gallery's curator David Scull was on site when I visited and I was lucky to meet the organiser of the competition Maggie Gowan by chance as she happened to drop in. I approached the gallery via a leafy street away from the hustle and bustle of the city. As I got closer I could see the large front window showcasing the winning photograph, I felt excited and could not wait to enter. Inside I saw that the photographs were neatly displayed, appearing in groups in some cases, whilst others appeared in rows drawing your eyes across the wall space. The winning photographs were presented in frames and the runners up were mounted. Each photo appeared in its competition section, with each section taking up a wall. Beneath each photo was information about the photo itself and a hundred word brief by the photographer. The section for young photographs was allocated downstairs. The minimalist layout of the gallery meant you were not distracted from the photos by unnecessary furniture or posters. I liked this layout and found it relaxing to view the exhibition. The lighting in the gallery was crisp and focused. Each individual photograph was lit by a spot light, this made the photographs attractive and drew you close to them. The gallery upstairs was very clean with polished wood flooring, white walls and the occasional red wall. I think that the exhibition was very good and I would definitely go there again. The content of the photos was interesting and inspiring. Some of the images had been captured in difficult situations. For example the photo of the mountain hare was taken after a long wait in the cold. The photo of the gannet, titled Adolescence was taken by abseiling down the side of a cliff! I think the bright lighting was perfect, drawing attention to every detail in the photos. My only criticism of the gallery was that some areas leading downstairs looked a little unfinished and dusty. My highlight of the day was talking to the organiser of the competition, Maggie Gowan who was helpful and very interested in why I was there; she also talked to my parents about the competition. Maggie was clearly enthusiastic about what she was doing and talked us through her motives for doing the exhibition as well as her love for photography. She told me that had enjoyed seeing fantastic photos of nature in magazines and papers and felt compelled to bring these together in an exhibition, creating the competition to do so. She kindly gave us the competition's book, this presents all the photos and tells us a little about all of them.', 'time': '2010-11-28', 'wordsCount': 483}]

name: Acculaser Skin Clinic
reviews: [{'language': 'en', 'polarity': 8, 'rating': 5, 'source': 'GooglePlaces', 'text': 'I went to Acculaser to have a spider angioma on my face treated. (This is a collection of thread veins that have a common centre - like a spider!). I thought it could turn into something malignant as it was increasingly hard to cover with make-up. I got a specific "deal" through Wowcher so I had a half price laser treatment (approx. Â£49). Too good an opportunity to pass up! I rang the clinic and got an appointment for 10 days hence, and I spoke directly to the clinician who asked about my requirements. She also gave me clear instructions on how to get to Acculaser. It's quite a discreet "shop front" so easy to miss unless you know what you are looking for. The clinic and reception areas are light, airy and spotlessly clean. The staff are helpful and clear. I had to fill in a health questionnaire which was passed to the clinician who talked me through my responses and possible risks - which were minimal in my case. The treatment itself does hurt a bit - like a sharp stinging sensation, but it is bearable. It took about 2 minutes. I was given clear advice and a post-treatment fact sheet, along with a number to call if I had any problems. Within a month, my spider angioma has completely vanished and I am really pleased with the treatment and subsequent results. I stick to high UVA/UVB sun protection and never go without it - even in the British sun. I wouldn't hesitate to recommend Acculaser. It's a thoroughly professional service, quick and thorough. Thank you!', 'time': '2013-07-29', 'wordsCount': 273}]
